**Ryo Kiyuna** (喜友名諒, _Kiyuna Ryō_, born 12 July 1990)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryo_Kiyuna#cite_note-karate_results_asian_games_2018-2) is an Okinawan [karateka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karate "Karate"). He won the gold medal in the [men's kata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karate_at_the_2020_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_kata "Karate at the 2020 Summer Olympics – Men's kata") event at the [2020 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Summer_Olympics "2020 Summer Olympics") in Tokyo, Japan.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryo_Kiyuna#cite_note-world_champion_kiyuna_wins_first_mens_olympic_kata_title_2021-3) He is also a four-time gold medalist in the men's kata event at the [World Karate Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Karate_Championships "World Karate Championships") and a two-time gold medalist in the men's team kata event, alongside [Arata Kinjo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arata_Kinjo "Arata Kinjo") and [Takuya Uemura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Takuya_Uemura "Takuya Uemura").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryo_Kiyuna#cite_note-remembering_world_karate_championships_2018-4) He has also won multiple gold medals in both the individual and team kata events at the [Asian Karate Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asian_Karate_Championships "Asian Karate Championships").

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ryo_Kiyuna&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Career")]

At the [2012 World Karate Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_World_Karate_Championships "2012 World Karate Championships") held in Paris, France, Kiyuna won one of the bronze medals in the men's individual kata event.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryo_Kiyuna#cite_note-tokyo_weekender_meet_sensation_tokyo_2020-5) The following year, he [represented Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_at_the_2013_World_Games "Japan at the 2013 World Games") at the [2013 World Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_World_Games "2013 World Games") in Cali, Colombia and he won the bronze medal in the [men's kata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karate_at_the_2013_World_Games "Karate at the 2013 World Games") event.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryo_Kiyuna#cite_note-karate_medalists_world_games_2013-6)

In 2014, at the [World Karate Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_World_Karate_Championships "2014 World Karate Championships") held in Bremen, Germany, Kiyuna won the gold medal in the men's individual kata event.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryo_Kiyuna#cite_note-tokyo_weekender_meet_sensation_tokyo_2020-5)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryo_Kiyuna#cite_note-four_gold_medals_opening_day_world_championships_2016-7) At the [2016 World Karate Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_World_Karate_Championships "2016 World Karate Championships") held in Linz, Austria, he won the gold medal in both the men's individual and men's team kata events.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryo_Kiyuna#cite_note-tokyo_weekender_meet_sensation_tokyo_2020-5)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryo_Kiyuna#cite_note-four_gold_medals_opening_day_world_championships_2016-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryo_Kiyuna#cite_note-japan_top_medal_table_world_2016-8) In 2017, Kiyuna won the gold medal in the [men's kata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karate_at_the_2017_World_Games_%E2%80%93_Men's_kata "Karate at the 2017 World Games – Men's kata") event at the [World Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_World_Games "2017 World Games") held in Wrocław, Poland.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryo_Kiyuna#cite_note-tokyo_weekender_meet_sensation_tokyo_2020-5)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryo_Kiyuna#cite_note-kiyuna_shimizu_gold_world_games_2017-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryo_Kiyuna#cite_note-karate_results_world_games_2017-10) In the final, he defeated [Damián Quintero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dami%C3%A1n_Quintero "Damián Quintero") of Spain.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryo_Kiyuna#cite_note-karate_results_world_games_2017-10)

At the [2018 Asian Karate Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_Asian_Karate_Championships "2018 Asian Karate Championships") held in Amman, Jordan, Kiyuna won the gold medal in the men's kata event.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryo_Kiyuna#cite_note-japan_claim_seven_gold_asian_karate_2018-11) A month later, he won the gold medal in the [men's kata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karate_at_the_2018_Asian_Games_%E2%80%93_Men's_kata "Karate at the 2018 Asian Games – Men's kata") event at the [2018 Asian Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_Asian_Games "2018 Asian Games") held in Jakarta, Indonesia.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryo_Kiyuna#cite_note-tokyo_weekender_meet_sensation_tokyo_2020-5)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryo_Kiyuna#cite_note-karate_results_asian_games_2018-2)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryo_Kiyuna#cite_note-unified_korean_team_dragon_boat_2018-12) In the final, he defeated [Wang Yi-ta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wang_Yi-ta "Wang Yi-ta") of Taiwan. In 2019, at the [Asian Karate Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_Asian_Karate_Championships "2019 Asian Karate Championships") held in Tashkent, Uzbekistan, he won the gold medal in both the men's individual kata and men's team kata events.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryo_Kiyuna#cite_note-japan_earn_six_titles_uzbek_golden_2019-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryo_Kiyuna#cite_note-asian_karate_championships_results_2019-14)

Kiyuna [represented Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_at_the_2020_Summer_Olympics "Japan at the 2020 Summer Olympics") at the [2020 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Summer_Olympics "2020 Summer Olympics") in Tokyo, Japan.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryo_Kiyuna#cite_note-wkf_announces_first_qualified_2020-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryo_Kiyuna#cite_note-wkf_announces_first_forty_tokyo_2020-16) event,[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryo_Kiyuna#cite_note-kiyuna_mesmerises_to_win_kata_gold_2021-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryo_Kiyuna#cite_note-karate_one_games_wonder_drama_emotion_tokyo_2020-18) becoming Japan's first gold medalist from Okinawa.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryo_Kiyuna#cite_note-olympics.com-19) In the final, he defeated [Damián Quintero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dami%C3%A1n_Quintero "Damián Quintero") of Spain.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryo_Kiyuna#cite_note-karate_results_book_summer_olympics_2020-20) He was ceremony").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryo_Kiyuna#cite_note-closing_ceremony_flag_bearers_summer_olympics_2020-21) A few months after the Olympics, he won the gold medal in the [men's kata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_World_Karate_Championships_%E2%80%93_Men's_individual_kata "2021 World Karate Championships – Men's individual kata") event at the [2021 World Karate Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_World_Karate_Championships "2021 World Karate Championships") held in Dubai, United Arab Emirates.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryo_Kiyuna#cite_note-kiyuna_makes_history_as_olympic_gold_medallists_retain_titles_karate_world_championships_2021-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryo_Kiyuna#cite_note-world_karate_championships_results_book_2021-23) In December 2021, he won the gold medal in both the men's individual and men's team kata events at the [Asian Karate Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Asian_Karate_Championships "2021 Asian Karate Championships") held in Almaty, Kazakhstan.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryo_Kiyuna#cite_note-japan_top_medal_table_asian_karate_championships_in_almaty_2021-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryo_Kiyuna#cite_note-results_book_asian_karate_championships_2021-25)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ryo_Kiyuna&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Personal life")]

He studied at [Okinawa International University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Okinawa_International_University "Okinawa International University").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryo_Kiyuna#cite_note-ryukyu_shimpo_determined_to_win_tokyo_2020-1) In December 2020, he contracted [COVID-19](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coronavirus_disease_2019 "Coronavirus disease 2019").[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryo_Kiyuna#cite_note-karate_world_kiyuna_contracts_coronavirus_2020-26)

Kiyuna's mother died in 2019 at the age of 57. At the gold medal ceremony for kata at the Tokyo 2020 Olympics, Kiyuna paid tribute to his mother's support by carrying a framed picture of her during the proceedings.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryo_Kiyuna#cite_note-wapost-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryo_Kiyuna#cite_note-kyodo-28)

**Damián Hugo Quintero Capdevila** (born 4 July 1984)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dami%C3%A1n_Quintero#cite_note-entry_list_by_noc_karate_world_games_2017-1) is a Spanish [karateka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karate "Karate"). He won the silver medal in the [men's kata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karate_at_the_2020_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_kata "Karate at the 2020 Summer Olympics – Men's kata") event at the [2020 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Summer_Olympics "2020 Summer Olympics") in Tokyo, Japan.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dami%C3%A1n_Quintero#cite_note-world_champion_kiyuna_wins_first_mens_olympic_kata_title_2021-2) He is also a four-time silver medalist in the individual kata event at the [World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Karate_Championships "World Karate Championships"), a seven-time gold medalist in his event at the [European Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Karate_Championships "European Karate Championships") and a three-time gold medalist in this event at the [European Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Games "European Games").

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dami%C3%A1n_Quintero&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Born in [Buenos Aires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buenos_Aires "Buenos Aires"), he emigrated with his family to [Torremolinos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torremolinos "Torremolinos"), [Malaga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%A1laga "Málaga"), [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain "Spain") a few years later.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dami%C3%A1n_Quintero#cite_note-3) He began his karate training in 1991, at a [Goju Ryu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goju_Ryu "Goju Ryu") school run by Lorenzo Marin. In 1997, he won the Spanish national championship children's category.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dami%C3%A1n_Quintero#cite_note-4)

In 2017, Quintero won the silver medal in the [individual kata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karate_at_the_2017_World_Games_%E2%80%93_Men's_kata "Karate at the 2017 World Games – Men's kata") event at the [World Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_World_Games "2017 World Games") held in [Wrocław](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wroc%C5%82aw "Wrocław"), [Poland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poland "Poland").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dami%C3%A1n_Quintero#cite_note-karate_results_world_games_2017-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dami%C3%A1n_Quintero#cite_note-netherlands_claim_ninth_title_in_row_2017-6)

In 2019, Quintero won the gold medal in the [men's individual kata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karate_at_the_2019_European_Games_%E2%80%93_Men's_individual_kata "Karate at the 2019 European Games – Men's individual kata") event at the [European Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_European_Games "2019 European Games") held in Minsk, Belarus.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dami%C3%A1n_Quintero#cite_note-spain_take_three_golds_minsk_2019-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dami%C3%A1n_Quintero#cite_note-karate_medalists_european_games_2019-8) In the same year, he won the gold medal in the men's kata event at the [European Karate Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_European_Karate_Championships "2019 European Karate Championships") held in [Guadalajara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guadalajara,_Spain "Guadalajara, Spain"), [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain "Spain").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dami%C3%A1n_Quintero#cite_note-results_book_european_karate_championships_2019-9) In the same year, he also won the gold medal in the [men's individual kata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karate_kata_at_the_2019_World_Beach_Games "Karate kata at the 2019 World Beach Games") event at the [World Beach Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_World_Beach_Games "2019 World Beach Games") held in [Doha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doha "Doha"), [Qatar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qatar "Qatar").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dami%C3%A1n_Quintero#cite_note-spain_celebrate_double_karate_gold_2019-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dami%C3%A1n_Quintero#cite_note-karate_results_book_world_beach_games_2019-11)

Quintero [represented Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain_at_the_2020_Summer_Olympics "Spain at the 2020 Summer Olympics") at the [2020 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Summer_Olympics "2020 Summer Olympics") in [Tokyo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokyo "Tokyo"), [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dami%C3%A1n_Quintero#cite_note-wkf_announces_first_qualified_2020-12) He won the silver medal in the [men's kata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karate_at_the_2020_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_kata "Karate at the 2020 Summer Olympics – Men's kata") event. A few months after the Olympics, he won the silver medal in the [men's kata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_World_Karate_Championships_%E2%80%93_Men's_individual_kata "2021 World Karate Championships – Men's individual kata") event at the [2021 World Karate Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_World_Karate_Championships "2021 World Karate Championships") held in [Dubai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dubai "Dubai"), [United Arab Emirates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates "United Arab Emirates").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dami%C3%A1n_Quintero#cite_note-kiyuna_makes_history_as_olympic_gold_medallists_retain_titles_karate_world_championships_2021-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dami%C3%A1n_Quintero#cite_note-world_karate_championships_results_book_2021-14)

Quintero won the silver medal in the [men's kata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karate_at_the_2022_World_Games_%E2%80%93_Men's_kata "Karate at the 2022 World Games – Men's kata") event at the [2022 World Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_World_Games "2022 World Games") held in [Birmingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham,_Alabama "Birmingham, Alabama"), [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dami%C3%A1n_Quintero#cite_note-karate_results_book_world_games_2022-15)

Quintero won the gold medal in the [men's individual kata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_European_Karate_Championships_%E2%80%93_Men's_individual_kata "2023 European Karate Championships – Men's individual kata") event at the [2023 European Karate Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_European_Karate_Championships "2023 European Karate Championships") held in [Guadalajara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guadalajara,_Spain "Guadalajara, Spain"), [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain "Spain"). He also won the gold medal in the [men's individual kata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karate_at_the_2023_European_Games_%E2%80%93_Men's_individual_kata "Karate at the 2023 European Games – Men's individual kata") event at the [2023 European Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_European_Games "2023 European Games") held in [Poland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poland "Poland").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dami%C3%A1n_Quintero#cite_note-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dami%C3%A1n_Quintero#cite_note-summary_day_one_european_games_2023-17) He won the silver medal in the [men's individual kata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_World_Karate_Championships_%E2%80%93_Men's_individual_kata "2023 World Karate Championships – Men's individual kata") event at the [2023 World Karate Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_World_Karate_Championships "2023 World Karate Championships") held in [Budapest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Budapest "Budapest"), [Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungary "Hungary").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dami%C3%A1n_Quintero#cite_note-world_karate_championships_results_book_2023-18)

**Damián Hugo Quintero Capdevila** (born 4 July 1984)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dami%C3%A1n_Quintero#cite_note-entry_list_by_noc_karate_world_games_2017-1) is a Spanish [karateka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karate "Karate"). He won the silver medal in the [men's kata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karate_at_the_2020_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_kata "Karate at the 2020 Summer Olympics – Men's kata") event at the [2020 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Summer_Olympics "2020 Summer Olympics") in Tokyo, Japan.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dami%C3%A1n_Quintero#cite_note-world_champion_kiyuna_wins_first_mens_olympic_kata_title_2021-2) He is also a four-time silver medalist in the individual kata event at the [World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Karate_Championships "World Karate Championships"), a seven-time gold medalist in his event at the [European Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Karate_Championships "European Karate Championships") and a three-time gold medalist in this event at the [European Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Games "European Games").

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dami%C3%A1n_Quintero&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Born in [Buenos Aires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buenos_Aires "Buenos Aires"), he emigrated with his family to [Torremolinos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torremolinos "Torremolinos"), [Malaga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%A1laga "Málaga"), [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain "Spain") a few years later.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dami%C3%A1n_Quintero#cite_note-3) He began his karate training in 1991, at a [Goju Ryu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goju_Ryu "Goju Ryu") school run by Lorenzo Marin. In 1997, he won the Spanish national championship children's category.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dami%C3%A1n_Quintero#cite_note-4)

In 2017, Quintero won the silver medal in the [individual kata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karate_at_the_2017_World_Games_%E2%80%93_Men's_kata "Karate at the 2017 World Games – Men's kata") event at the [World Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_World_Games "2017 World Games") held in [Wrocław](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wroc%C5%82aw "Wrocław"), [Poland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poland "Poland").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dami%C3%A1n_Quintero#cite_note-karate_results_world_games_2017-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dami%C3%A1n_Quintero#cite_note-netherlands_claim_ninth_title_in_row_2017-6)

In 2019, Quintero won the gold medal in the [men's individual kata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karate_at_the_2019_European_Games_%E2%80%93_Men's_individual_kata "Karate at the 2019 European Games – Men's individual kata") event at the [European Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_European_Games "2019 European Games") held in Minsk, Belarus.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dami%C3%A1n_Quintero#cite_note-spain_take_three_golds_minsk_2019-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dami%C3%A1n_Quintero#cite_note-karate_medalists_european_games_2019-8) In the same year, he won the gold medal in the men's kata event at the [European Karate Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_European_Karate_Championships "2019 European Karate Championships") held in [Guadalajara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guadalajara,_Spain "Guadalajara, Spain"), [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain "Spain").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dami%C3%A1n_Quintero#cite_note-results_book_european_karate_championships_2019-9) In the same year, he also won the gold medal in the [men's individual kata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karate_kata_at_the_2019_World_Beach_Games "Karate kata at the 2019 World Beach Games") event at the [World Beach Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_World_Beach_Games "2019 World Beach Games") held in [Doha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doha "Doha"), [Qatar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qatar "Qatar").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dami%C3%A1n_Quintero#cite_note-spain_celebrate_double_karate_gold_2019-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dami%C3%A1n_Quintero#cite_note-karate_results_book_world_beach_games_2019-11)

Quintero [represented Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain_at_the_2020_Summer_Olympics "Spain at the 2020 Summer Olympics") at the [2020 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Summer_Olympics "2020 Summer Olympics") in [Tokyo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokyo "Tokyo"), [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dami%C3%A1n_Quintero#cite_note-wkf_announces_first_qualified_2020-12) He won the silver medal in the [men's kata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karate_at_the_2020_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_kata "Karate at the 2020 Summer Olympics – Men's kata") event. A few months after the Olympics, he won the silver medal in the [men's kata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_World_Karate_Championships_%E2%80%93_Men's_individual_kata "2021 World Karate Championships – Men's individual kata") event at the [2021 World Karate Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_World_Karate_Championships "2021 World Karate Championships") held in [Dubai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dubai "Dubai"), [United Arab Emirates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates "United Arab Emirates").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dami%C3%A1n_Quintero#cite_note-kiyuna_makes_history_as_olympic_gold_medallists_retain_titles_karate_world_championships_2021-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dami%C3%A1n_Quintero#cite_note-world_karate_championships_results_book_2021-14)

Quintero won the silver medal in the [men's kata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karate_at_the_2022_World_Games_%E2%80%93_Men's_kata "Karate at the 2022 World Games – Men's kata") event at the [2022 World Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_World_Games "2022 World Games") held in [Birmingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham,_Alabama "Birmingham, Alabama"), [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dami%C3%A1n_Quintero#cite_note-karate_results_book_world_games_2022-15)

Quintero won the gold medal in the [men's individual kata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_European_Karate_Championships_%E2%80%93_Men's_individual_kata "2023 European Karate Championships – Men's individual kata") event at the [2023 European Karate Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_European_Karate_Championships "2023 European Karate Championships") held in [Guadalajara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guadalajara,_Spain "Guadalajara, Spain"), [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain "Spain"). He also won the gold medal in the [men's individual kata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karate_at_the_2023_European_Games_%E2%80%93_Men's_individual_kata "Karate at the 2023 European Games – Men's individual kata") event at the [2023 European Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_European_Games "2023 European Games") held in [Poland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poland "Poland").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dami%C3%A1n_Quintero#cite_note-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dami%C3%A1n_Quintero#cite_note-summary_day_one_european_games_2023-17) He won the silver medal in the [men's individual kata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_World_Karate_Championships_%E2%80%93_Men's_individual_kata "2023 World Karate Championships – Men's individual kata") event at the [2023 World Karate Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_World_Karate_Championships "2023 World Karate Championships") held in [Budapest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Budapest "Budapest"), [Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungary "Hungary").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dami%C3%A1n_Quintero#cite_note-world_karate_championships_results_book_2023-18)

**[Taekwondo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taekwondo "Taekwondo")** at the **[2016 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Summer_Olympics "2016 Summer Olympics")** in [Rio de Janeiro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rio_de_Janeiro "Rio de Janeiro") took place from 17 to 20 August at the [Carioca Arena 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carioca_Arena_3 "Carioca Arena 3") inside the [Barra Olympic Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barra_Olympic_Park "Barra Olympic Park") in [Barra da Tijuca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barra_da_Tijuca "Barra da Tijuca"). Around 128 taekwondo fighters competed in eight weight categories; four for men, and four for women.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taekwondo_at_the_2016_Summer_Olympics#cite_note-1)

## Qualification

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Taekwondo_at_the_2016_Summer_Olympics&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Qualification")]

Main article: [Taekwondo at the 2016 Summer Olympics – Qualification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taekwondo_at_the_2016_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Qualification "Taekwondo at the 2016 Summer Olympics – Qualification")

Taekwondo competition at these Games featured a total of 128 athletes, 64 in each gender, and 16 in each of the eight weight categories. Each [National Olympic Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Olympic_Committee "National Olympic Committee") (NOC) was allowed to enter up to a maximum of eight competitors, four of each gender, based on the World Taekwondo Federation (WTF) Olympic rankings, such that an athlete per NOC must be among the top six in each weight category. If an NOC had qualified only two female and male athletes through ranking, it could not participate in the respective Continental Qualification Tournament unless it had relinquishing the places obtained through ranking.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taekwondo_at_the_2016_Summer_Olympics#cite_note-wtf-qual-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taekwondo_at_the_2016_Summer_Olympics#cite_note-3)

Four places had been reserved to the host nation [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil_at_the_2016_Summer_Olympics "Brazil at the 2016 Summer Olympics"), and another four had been invited by the Tripartite Commission. The remaining 120 places were allocated through a qualification process in which athletes had won quota place for their respective NOC. 48 taekwondo fighters, 24 in each gender and the top 6 in each weight category, were eligible to compete through the ITTF Olympic rankings, while the rest through the five Continental Qualification Tournaments.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taekwondo_at_the_2016_Summer_Olympics#cite_note-wtf-qual-2)

If an NOC having qualified through a Qualification Tournament relinquishing a quota place, it would be allocated to the nation of the next highest placed athlete in the respective weight category of that tournament as long as the addition of the place did not exceed the maximum quota for that nation.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taekwondo_at_the_2016_Summer_Olympics#cite_note-wtf-qual-2)

**[Taekwondo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taekwondo "Taekwondo")** at the **[2016 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Summer_Olympics "2016 Summer Olympics")** in [Rio de Janeiro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rio_de_Janeiro "Rio de Janeiro") took place from 17 to 20 August at the [Carioca Arena 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carioca_Arena_3 "Carioca Arena 3") inside the [Barra Olympic Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barra_Olympic_Park "Barra Olympic Park") in [Barra da Tijuca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barra_da_Tijuca "Barra da Tijuca"). Around 128 taekwondo fighters competed in eight weight categories; four for men, and four for women.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taekwondo_at_the_2016_Summer_Olympics#cite_note-1)

## Qualification

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Taekwondo_at_the_2016_Summer_Olympics&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Qualification")]

Main article: [Taekwondo at the 2016 Summer Olympics – Qualification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taekwondo_at_the_2016_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Qualification "Taekwondo at the 2016 Summer Olympics – Qualification")

Taekwondo competition at these Games featured a total of 128 athletes, 64 in each gender, and 16 in each of the eight weight categories. Each [National Olympic Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Olympic_Committee "National Olympic Committee") (NOC) was allowed to enter up to a maximum of eight competitors, four of each gender, based on the World Taekwondo Federation (WTF) Olympic rankings, such that an athlete per NOC must be among the top six in each weight category. If an NOC had qualified only two female and male athletes through ranking, it could not participate in the respective Continental Qualification Tournament unless it had relinquishing the places obtained through ranking.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taekwondo_at_the_2016_Summer_Olympics#cite_note-wtf-qual-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taekwondo_at_the_2016_Summer_Olympics#cite_note-3)

Four places had been reserved to the host nation [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil_at_the_2016_Summer_Olympics "Brazil at the 2016 Summer Olympics"), and another four had been invited by the Tripartite Commission. The remaining 120 places were allocated through a qualification process in which athletes had won quota place for their respective NOC. 48 taekwondo fighters, 24 in each gender and the top 6 in each weight category, were eligible to compete through the ITTF Olympic rankings, while the rest through the five Continental Qualification Tournaments.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taekwondo_at_the_2016_Summer_Olympics#cite_note-wtf-qual-2)

If an NOC having qualified through a Qualification Tournament relinquishing a quota place, it would be allocated to the nation of the next highest placed athlete in the respective weight category of that tournament as long as the addition of the place did not exceed the maximum quota for that nation.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taekwondo_at_the_2016_Summer_Olympics#cite_note-wtf-qual-2)

**Mohammed Mustafa Shehab** (born 11 December 1976) is a former professional [snooker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snooker "Snooker") player from the [United Arab Emirates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates "United Arab Emirates").

The winner of the Snooker Singles at the [2007 Asian Indoor Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_Asian_Indoor_Games "2007 Asian Indoor Games"), Shehab has enjoyed good form in [six-red snooker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Six-red_snooker "Six-red snooker"), most notably at the [2018 Six-red World Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_Six-red_World_Championship "2018 Six-red World Championship"), where he reached the quarter-finals, defeating reigning [World Champion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_World_Snooker_Championship "2018 World Snooker Championship")[Mark Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Williams_(snooker_player) "Mark Williams (snooker player)") in the last 16.

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mohammed_Shehab&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Career")]

He competed as a professional on the [main tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Snooker_Tour "World Snooker Tour") in the [1996–97](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996%E2%80%9397_snooker_season "1996–97 snooker season") and [2006–07](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006%E2%80%9307_snooker_season "2006–07 snooker season") seasons, finishing the latter with a [ranking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snooker_world_rankings "Snooker world rankings") of 90th, the highest of his career.

Shehab regained the professional status recently in Q Tour Global Playoffs after defeating Hong Kong China’s Yu Kiu Chang 10-8 to earn a third spell on the World Snooker Tour.

### Main tour

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mohammed_Shehab&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Main tour")]

He entered nine tournaments, but his best performances came in the 1997 International Open and the European Open, where he reached the third qualifying round. Shehab had recorded his first professional win in the former, a 5–3 defeat of Englishman Rajan Sharma, but added only five more all season. Shebab would participate in the qualifying for both the [1996 UK Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_UK_Championship "1996 UK Championship") and the [1997 World Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997_World_Snooker_Championship "1997 World Snooker Championship"). His season's campaign culminated in a 1–5 loss to Iain Trimble in his second match. He finished the season ranked 397th and, with the addition of the secondary [UK Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Q_Tour "Q Tour"), was immediately relegated from the main tour.

Shehab did not play again competitively for five years, until he entered the 2002 World Amateur Championship. There, he compensated for losses to [Martin Gould](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Gould "Martin Gould") and [Alex Borg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Borg_(snooker_player) "Alex Borg (snooker player)") with victories over Habib Subah and seven others to progress from his group. He beat [Supoj Saenla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supoj_Saenla "Supoj Saenla") and Martin McCrudden to reach the quarter-finals, but lost 5–6 there to [Steve Mifsud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Mifsud "Steve Mifsud").

This led Shehab to enter several events on the [Challenge Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenge_Tour_(snooker) "Challenge Tour (snooker)"), which had replaced the UK Tour, during the 2003/2004 season; he lost in the semi-finals of one event to [Stefan Mazrocis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stefan_Mazrocis "Stefan Mazrocis"), but progressed no further after this. In Event Two, he defeated seventeen-year-old [Mark Allen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Allen_(snooker_player) "Mark Allen (snooker player)") 4–3, but lost to [Steve James](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_James_(snooker_player) "Steve James (snooker player)") in his next match. Shehab would also attempt to qualify for the world championship this season, but lose in the second round of qualifying to [Lee Farebrother](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Farebrother?action=edit&redlink=1 "Lee Farebrother (page does not exist)")

Although he entered only one tournament in the following two seasons - losing 1–4 to [Andrew Higginson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Higginson_(snooker_player) "Andrew Higginson (snooker player)") in Event 1 of the 2004 Challenge Tour - Shehab won back his place on the main tour in 2006.

His second season as a professional brought no more success than his first, Shehab winning only four matches and earning only £500. He defeated [Stuart Pettman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stuart_Pettman "Stuart Pettman"), [Liu Song](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liu_Song_(snooker_player) "Liu Song (snooker player)") and Borg in the 2006 Grand Prix, and Liu again in the Malta Cup, but lost his final four matches. Following a 6–10 loss to [Mark Joyce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Joyce "Mark Joyce") in qualifying for the [2007 World Snooker Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_World_Snooker_Championship "2007 World Snooker Championship"), Shehab finished the season ranked 90th, and was relegated once more from the tour.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_Shehab#cite_note-2)

### Amateur career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mohammed_Shehab&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Amateur career")]

Shehab would later win the [Singles Snooker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cue_sports_at_the_2007_Asian_Indoor_Games "Cue sports at the 2007 Asian Indoor Games") championship at the [2007 Asian Indoor Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_Asian_Indoor_Games "2007 Asian Indoor Games"). He defeated India's [Yasin Merchant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yasin_Merchant "Yasin Merchant") 4–2, Hong Kong's [Chan Wai Ki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chan_Wai_Ki "Chan Wai Ki") 4–1, Thailand's [Issara Kachaiwong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Issara_Kachaiwong "Issara Kachaiwong") 4–1, China's [Xiao Guodong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xiao_Guodong "Xiao Guodong") 4–3 before beating Thailand's [James Wattana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Wattana "James Wattana") 4–3 in the final.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_Shehab#cite_note-3)

After playing as a wildcard entry in the [2009 Shanghai Masters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_Shanghai_Masters "2009 Shanghai Masters"), losing 3–5 to [Graeme Dott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graeme_Dott "Graeme Dott"), Shebab would contest the [2009 Six-red World Grand Prix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_Six-red_World_Grand_Prix "2009 Six-red World Grand Prix"), where he would come second in his group, defeating [Joe Perry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Perry_(snooker_player) "Joe Perry (snooker player)"), and eventual winner [Jimmy White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_White "Jimmy White"), before defeating [Nigel Bond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigel_Bond "Nigel Bond") in the first round. He would lose his second knockout round match to [Judd Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judd_Trump "Judd Trump").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_Shehab#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_Shehab#cite_note-Global_Snooker-5)

After 2009, Shehab continued to play at amateur level, entering the World Amateur Championship each year. His best performance came during the 2013 edition, when he reached the quarter-finals, where [Lee Walker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Walker "Lee Walker") beat him 6–3.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_Shehab#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_Shehab#cite_note-7) Shebab would make an appearance in the [2018 Six-red World Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_Six-red_World_Championship "2018 Six-red World Championship"), where he would qualify from his group, thanks to wins over [David Gilbert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Gilbert_(snooker_player) "David Gilbert (snooker player)")[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_Shehab#cite_note-8) and [Thanawat Tirapongpaiboon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thanawat_Tirapongpaiboon "Thanawat Tirapongpaiboon"),[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_Shehab#cite_note-9) and a 5–4 loss to [Mark Selby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Selby "Mark Selby").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_Shehab#cite_note-2018_six_red-10) Shehab would draw world snooker champion [Mark Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Williams_(snooker_player) "Mark Williams (snooker player)") in the last 16 knockout round.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_Shehab#cite_note-2018_six_red-10) Shehab would win the match 6–3, and would play [Sunny Akani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunny_Akani "Sunny Akani") in the Quarter-finals.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_Shehab#cite_note-results-11)

**Mohammed Mustafa Shehab** (born 11 December 1976) is a former professional [snooker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snooker "Snooker") player from the [United Arab Emirates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates "United Arab Emirates").

The winner of the Snooker Singles at the [2007 Asian Indoor Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_Asian_Indoor_Games "2007 Asian Indoor Games"), Shehab has enjoyed good form in [six-red snooker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Six-red_snooker "Six-red snooker"), most notably at the [2018 Six-red World Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_Six-red_World_Championship "2018 Six-red World Championship"), where he reached the quarter-finals, defeating reigning [World Champion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_World_Snooker_Championship "2018 World Snooker Championship")[Mark Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Williams_(snooker_player) "Mark Williams (snooker player)") in the last 16.

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mohammed_Shehab&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Career")]

He competed as a professional on the [main tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Snooker_Tour "World Snooker Tour") in the [1996–97](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996%E2%80%9397_snooker_season "1996–97 snooker season") and [2006–07](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006%E2%80%9307_snooker_season "2006–07 snooker season") seasons, finishing the latter with a [ranking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snooker_world_rankings "Snooker world rankings") of 90th, the highest of his career.

Shehab regained the professional status recently in Q Tour Global Playoffs after defeating Hong Kong China’s Yu Kiu Chang 10-8 to earn a third spell on the World Snooker Tour.

### Main tour

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mohammed_Shehab&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Main tour")]

He entered nine tournaments, but his best performances came in the 1997 International Open and the European Open, where he reached the third qualifying round. Shehab had recorded his first professional win in the former, a 5–3 defeat of Englishman Rajan Sharma, but added only five more all season. Shebab would participate in the qualifying for both the [1996 UK Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_UK_Championship "1996 UK Championship") and the [1997 World Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997_World_Snooker_Championship "1997 World Snooker Championship"). His season's campaign culminated in a 1–5 loss to Iain Trimble in his second match. He finished the season ranked 397th and, with the addition of the secondary [UK Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Q_Tour "Q Tour"), was immediately relegated from the main tour.

Shehab did not play again competitively for five years, until he entered the 2002 World Amateur Championship. There, he compensated for losses to [Martin Gould](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Gould "Martin Gould") and [Alex Borg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Borg_(snooker_player) "Alex Borg (snooker player)") with victories over Habib Subah and seven others to progress from his group. He beat [Supoj Saenla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supoj_Saenla "Supoj Saenla") and Martin McCrudden to reach the quarter-finals, but lost 5–6 there to [Steve Mifsud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Mifsud "Steve Mifsud").

This led Shehab to enter several events on the [Challenge Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenge_Tour_(snooker) "Challenge Tour (snooker)"), which had replaced the UK Tour, during the 2003/2004 season; he lost in the semi-finals of one event to [Stefan Mazrocis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stefan_Mazrocis "Stefan Mazrocis"), but progressed no further after this. In Event Two, he defeated seventeen-year-old [Mark Allen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Allen_(snooker_player) "Mark Allen (snooker player)") 4–3, but lost to [Steve James](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_James_(snooker_player) "Steve James (snooker player)") in his next match. Shehab would also attempt to qualify for the world championship this season, but lose in the second round of qualifying to [Lee Farebrother](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Farebrother?action=edit&redlink=1 "Lee Farebrother (page does not exist)")

Although he entered only one tournament in the following two seasons - losing 1–4 to [Andrew Higginson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Higginson_(snooker_player) "Andrew Higginson (snooker player)") in Event 1 of the 2004 Challenge Tour - Shehab won back his place on the main tour in 2006.

His second season as a professional brought no more success than his first, Shehab winning only four matches and earning only £500. He defeated [Stuart Pettman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stuart_Pettman "Stuart Pettman"), [Liu Song](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liu_Song_(snooker_player) "Liu Song (snooker player)") and Borg in the 2006 Grand Prix, and Liu again in the Malta Cup, but lost his final four matches. Following a 6–10 loss to [Mark Joyce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Joyce "Mark Joyce") in qualifying for the [2007 World Snooker Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_World_Snooker_Championship "2007 World Snooker Championship"), Shehab finished the season ranked 90th, and was relegated once more from the tour.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_Shehab#cite_note-2)

### Amateur career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mohammed_Shehab&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Amateur career")]

Shehab would later win the [Singles Snooker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cue_sports_at_the_2007_Asian_Indoor_Games "Cue sports at the 2007 Asian Indoor Games") championship at the [2007 Asian Indoor Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_Asian_Indoor_Games "2007 Asian Indoor Games"). He defeated India's [Yasin Merchant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yasin_Merchant "Yasin Merchant") 4–2, Hong Kong's [Chan Wai Ki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chan_Wai_Ki "Chan Wai Ki") 4–1, Thailand's [Issara Kachaiwong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Issara_Kachaiwong "Issara Kachaiwong") 4–1, China's [Xiao Guodong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xiao_Guodong "Xiao Guodong") 4–3 before beating Thailand's [James Wattana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Wattana "James Wattana") 4–3 in the final.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_Shehab#cite_note-3)

After playing as a wildcard entry in the [2009 Shanghai Masters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_Shanghai_Masters "2009 Shanghai Masters"), losing 3–5 to [Graeme Dott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graeme_Dott "Graeme Dott"), Shebab would contest the [2009 Six-red World Grand Prix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_Six-red_World_Grand_Prix "2009 Six-red World Grand Prix"), where he would come second in his group, defeating [Joe Perry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Perry_(snooker_player) "Joe Perry (snooker player)"), and eventual winner [Jimmy White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_White "Jimmy White"), before defeating [Nigel Bond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigel_Bond "Nigel Bond") in the first round. He would lose his second knockout round match to [Judd Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judd_Trump "Judd Trump").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_Shehab#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_Shehab#cite_note-Global_Snooker-5)

After 2009, Shehab continued to play at amateur level, entering the World Amateur Championship each year. His best performance came during the 2013 edition, when he reached the quarter-finals, where [Lee Walker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Walker "Lee Walker") beat him 6–3.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_Shehab#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_Shehab#cite_note-7) Shebab would make an appearance in the [2018 Six-red World Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_Six-red_World_Championship "2018 Six-red World Championship"), where he would qualify from his group, thanks to wins over [David Gilbert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Gilbert_(snooker_player) "David Gilbert (snooker player)")[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_Shehab#cite_note-8) and [Thanawat Tirapongpaiboon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thanawat_Tirapongpaiboon "Thanawat Tirapongpaiboon"),[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_Shehab#cite_note-9) and a 5–4 loss to [Mark Selby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Selby "Mark Selby").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_Shehab#cite_note-2018_six_red-10) Shehab would draw world snooker champion [Mark Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Williams_(snooker_player) "Mark Williams (snooker player)") in the last 16 knockout round.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_Shehab#cite_note-2018_six_red-10) Shehab would win the match 6–3, and would play [Sunny Akani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunny_Akani "Sunny Akani") in the Quarter-finals.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammed_Shehab#cite_note-results-11)
